article_markdown:
# Stop paying for stale job details

A customer sends a new address. The message reaches the office, but the live job still shows the old one. The field crew follows the job record, reaches the wrong gate and starts calling for clarification. The van moved, paid field time was used and the customer is still waiting.

The information arrived, but the process treated it as a message rather than a controlled change to an active job. This is the kind of operational leak Run Lighter is built to fix.

Field service job detail updates deserve their own workflow. A changed address, access note, contact, arrival window or site instruction should move into the record used to dispatch and perform the work. The people affected should see the change before they rely on it, and consequential updates should stop for human confirmation.

## A message is not the job record

Customer changes often arrive through whatever channel is easiest at the time: a text to the owner, a reply to a booking email, a call to reception or a note left with an account manager. Each channel may be valid for communication. The problem begins when the message becomes the only current version of the job.

Forwarding it to a group chat does not create a dependable source of truth. Someone still has to decide which job it belongs to, whether the customer is authorised to make the change, what old detail is being replaced and who must act on it.

This is different from [customer progress updates](/blog/silence-creates-avoidable-follow-up/). A progress update moves approved information from the operation to the customer. This workflow moves a customer change into the operation before people rely on stale details.

## 1. Choose one controlled route

Start with the job system the field team already trusts. Define how a change received by email, phone, form or text becomes a proposed update to that record.

The route does not need to force every customer into one communication channel. It needs to give staff one consistent action after the change arrives. That action might open a short change form, create a review task or prepare a draft update linked to the correct job.

Capture only what is required:

- the job or customer record
- the field being changed
- the previous value and proposed value
- where the change came from and when
- who is responsible for confirming it

Those details make the change reviewable. A screenshot buried in a private phone does not.

## 2. Update the record people actually use

A workflow should not create another list beside the job system. Once an approved change is confirmed, update the live record used for scheduling, dispatch and service delivery.

Then alert only the people who rely on that field. An address or access change may need the scheduler and assigned crew. A billing contact change may belong with administration. A scope change may need the job owner before anyone else acts.

The alert should identify what changed and link back to the controlled record. Avoid sending a full copy of customer information to every channel merely because the software can.

This same discipline helps when [the same customer detail is being typed twice](/blog/stop-typing-the-same-detail-twice/). One approved change should flow to the necessary places without creating several competing versions.

## 3. Make acknowledgement visible

Delivery is not the same as acknowledgement. A notification can reach a device while the assigned person is driving, working or offline.

For changes that affect the next visit, make acknowledgement visible before dispatch. The job record might show who has seen the update, when it was confirmed and whether a scheduler must follow up. If acknowledgement is missing near the point of use, create a task for the responsible person rather than sending repeated messages to everyone.

Keep the logic narrow. The system can show that the crew received the new address. It cannot assume they understand an unusual access risk or that the new timing remains commercially workable.

## 4. Stop consequential changes for a person

Not every field should update automatically. A person should confirm a change that affects:

- scope, price or payment terms
- safety, site conditions or required equipment
- access permissions, keys or security codes
- staffing or scheduling commitments
- regulatory, contractual or insurance requirements
- an unclear request or conflicting customer instruction

The workflow should bring the proposed change, original detail and relevant job context to the responsible person. That reduces searching without transferring judgement to software.

A useful exception path is explicit: who reviews it, what they may approve, how the customer is contacted and what happens if the change cannot be accepted.

## 5. Protect customer and site information

Addresses, phone numbers, access instructions and site notes can be personal or sensitive in context. Use approved systems, limit access to people who need the information and avoid copying complete records into loosely controlled chats.

For organisations covered by the Australian Privacy Principles, the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner’s current [APP 10 guidance](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-10-app-10-quality-of-personal-information) says reasonable steps are required to ensure personal information collected is accurate, up to date and complete, and that information used or disclosed is accurate, up to date, complete and relevant for the purpose. The guidance includes promptly adding updated information to relevant existing records as an example of a reasonable step.

The Australian Signals Directorate’s [customer data guidance](https://www.cyber.gov.au/business-government/small-business-cyber-security/securing-customer-personal-data) recommends understanding where customer data is held, limiting unnecessary duplication, consolidating repositories where appropriate, controlling access, and logging and monitoring access.

Apply those principles to the business’s circumstances and obtain professional advice where obligations are unclear. The operational goal is simple: current information should reach the people authorised to use it without spreading extra copies.

## 6. Test the ugly cases

Take several recent customer changes, including one that arrived late and one that was ambiguous. Follow each from the original message to the person who performed the work.

Test what happens when the job number is missing, two customers have similar names, the assigned crew changes, a device is offline, the customer sends conflicting updates or the proposed change arrives after dispatch.

Also test reversals. If a customer returns to the original address or time, the audit trail should show what changed, who approved it and which version is current.

Start with one category, such as address and access updates. Expand only after staff can see the current detail, the history and the exception owner without checking several channels.

## What remains under human judgement

People decide whether a consequential change is valid, safe, affordable and consistent with the promise already made. They handle uncertainty, negotiate scope and timing, and speak with customers when an update cannot be accepted.

Automation can collect the change, prepare the record, route it for approval, update approved systems and make acknowledgement visible. It should not guess which customer instruction wins or silently commit the business to new work.
